blocks: Aemilianus, proclaimed emperor, wrote to the senate: "I leave the empire to you, and I, your general, will fight for you everywhere."
text: Aemilianus, proclaimed emperor, wrote to the senate: "I leave the empire to you, and I, your general, will fight for you everywhere."

blocks: Macrinus, count of the treasuries and in charge of the corn market, since he was also lame in one foot, was not found in the war, but at Samosata, where he received the soldiers and restored them. Shapur sent Cledonius, the man who brought the judges in to the emperor, who urged Macrinus to come to Valerian. He chose not to go, saying: "Who is so mad as to become, of his own will, a slave and a captive instead of a free man? Besides, those who order me to go are not my masters. For one is an enemy, and the other is not even master of himself, let alone of us (to us, Mai)." And he urged Cledonius too to stay and not go back to Valerian. He said that he would not betray his loyalty to the man who had been his master. And going back, he was held with the captives.

blocks: Memor the Moor, sent to collect the crops, longed for revolution, and was quickly killed by the soldiers. The officers complained that he had been killed unjustly. And Theodotus, ordered to defend himself, said: "Memor did not deserve much condemnation as a man attempting the impossible, he who had the backing and power of so many officers; but he and those with him failed of their aim through my zeal and the emperor's foresight." The emperor, pleased with the defence, ordered that no one should be prosecuted on Memor's account. Men badly brought up do not usually keep their friendships firmly, but change them on small pretexts.

blocks: 1. The wife of the emperor Gallienus disliked the face of Ingenuus, and sending for Valentinus she said to him: "I know your loyalty, and I praise the emperor for choosing you, but for choosing Ingenuus I do not praise him. I hold him in deep suspicion; but I cannot act against the emperor; so you watch the man." Valentinus answered: "May Ingenuus too be found true in your service; for my part I shall leave nothing undone that looks to the goodwill of your house." 2. In the war against Ingenuus they killed many, sons and fathers and brothers, so much so that one man brought his own brother before Gallienus and said: "Emperor, this is my brother, and I took him in the war." Gallienus, thinking he wished to plead for him, received him and praised him, and promised to give him much and to forgive the crime of the usurpation. But the man said that one who had once taken up arms against the emperor ought not to live, and killed him with his sword. Gallienus was angry, yet because the thing was so unexpected he let it pass. 3. Claudius happened to be wounded in the ankle, and the emperor asked after him with great concern. One of the soldiers said that, having fought nobly like Achilles, he had been wounded, and was being cared for in his quarters; so that the emperor said that it was fitting he had been wounded in the ankle too.

blocks: The emperor Gallienus sent to Postumus, who had been proclaimed emperor, envoys who knew what he had done, to tell him that he ought to take the strongholds and keep quiet. "But let me come in, so that we may settle it between us; and the better man will be emperor." Postumus replied: "I will never willingly let you cross the Alps, nor do I pray to be brought to such a need that I should make war on Romans." Gallienus sent to him: "Then let us both fight in single combat, so that Romans may not perish." He replied: "I am not a gladiator, nor have I ever been one; but these provinces, which were being lost, I was appointed by you to save, and I saved them; and I was chosen emperor by the Gauls; and I am content to rule those who chose me of their own will; and if I can do anything by my counsel and my strength, I help them."

blocks: Rufinus killed the elder Odaenathus as one attempting revolution. The younger Odaenathus accused Rufinus of having murdered his father. The emperor asked Rufinus why he had done this. He said that he had done it with justice: "For he was attempting revolution; and I wish you had let me kill this Odaenathus too, his son, and I would have done it at once." Rufinus suffered from gout in his feet and hands, and could not move at all. And the emperor said to him: "Trusting in what strength and what body do you say this?" He said: "Not even if I had been healthy, beyond my youth, could I have done anything to him with my body; but by your right hand, ordering and arranging, I accomplished everything. For you yourself, emperor, do not act by the strength of your body, but by commanding your soldiers." And Gallienus praised his words.

blocks: 1. Quietus, the son of Macrinus, sat on the throne at Emesa (and at once), and Odaenathus came with a host of barbarians and told them: "Hand yourselves over, or fight." They said that they would endure anything at all rather than hand themselves over to a barbarian. 2. Carinus was vexed that Odaenathus had taken the war of the Romans on himself. Odaenathus, learning this, ordered him to be killed; and he lavished much from his own means on his burial, which he even showed him while he was alive. Carinus laughed and said the man was full of great ignorance and folly: ignorance, because we kill our enemies but show favour to our friends, and he did not know whether he was ranking him among friends or enemies; folly, because he wished to grieve and murder him while he lived and felt it, but to honour him with gifts when he was dead and felt nothing. And so great a good fortune had a swift reversal.

blocks: 1. When the Scythians had taken Athens in the time of Claudius and had gathered all the books and wished to burn them, another among them, thought to be wise, stopped them, saying that it is in these that the Romans spend their leisure and neglect war. He said this out of ignorance; for if he had known the virtues of the Athenians and the Romans, who won fame both in letters and in wars, he would not have said it. 2. The Scythians jeered at those shut up in cities, that they did not live a human life, but that of birds sitting high in nests; and that they left the earth that feeds them and chose barren cities; and that they trusted lifeless things more than themselves. 3. There was one Andonnoballus, who had deserted from the Heruli to the Romans. And he came to talk with Bibulus (the king) of the Romans. For he was urging him to give himself up to the emperor. The other called him a slave who loved his master and a slave to his belly, and said that he had lost his freedom for the sake of food and clothing (and bellyful?). He answered him: "I am free; for I am the friend of so great an emperor, and I lack none of the good things; but you have plenty of neither clothing nor food." 4. After the victory over the Scythians, when the emperor was celebrating and feasting, Andonnoballus came in before them all and said: "I want to ask a favour of you." And thinking he was about to ask for something great, the emperor let him ask. And Andonnoballus said: "Give me good wine, so that I may call all the people of my house and celebrate with them." And the emperor laughed and ordered wine to be given him; and he also gave him many other gifts.

blocks: 1. Aurelian, having become emperor and gathered all the men of note at Ravenna, took counsel how he ought to reign; for he wished, after the death of Claudius, to appear greater than him by what he did. One of the senate said to him: "If you want to reign well, fortify yourself with gold and iron: iron against those who trouble you, gold for those who serve you." And the man who gave this evil (most evil? his own, Zon.) advice was himself the first to enjoy it. 2. Albinus, an old man, was mortally ill; someone came in and asked him how he was. He said: "If the fatherland is safe, badly, for I am certainly dying; but if it is not safe, well, for I die before I learn of my fatherland's ruin; and I ask no greater good than this." 3. Aurelian, learning that a body of the barbarians was at Placentia, sent them word: "If you want to fight, here I am, ready; but if you think the better course is to give yourselves up, I receive you as your master." They replied: "We have no master; get yourself ready tomorrow, and you will learn that you are fighting free men." 4. Aurelian, while besieging Tyana, had told the soldiers: "If we get in, do not leave even a dog alive." After the city was taken he forbade the soldiers either to kill or to plunder. So the soldiers said to him in anger: "Let us do what you promised." And he said to them: "You speak the truth, that I said it: go, let no dog be found in this city; kill them all." And he sent the tribunes and the soldiers, and they killed all the dogs; so that the army's anger turned to laughter (melted away?). And after this he called them together and said: "We are fighting to free these cities; and if we are going to plunder them, they will no longer trust us; let us rather seek the barbarians' plunder, and spare these (these?) as our own." 5. Aurelian sent envoys to Zenobia, urging her to agree to be subject to him. She replied: "I have suffered no great harm; for those who fell in the war are almost all Romans." 6. Aurelian, once faced with a mutiny of the soldiers, said that the soldiers deceived themselves if they supposed that the fates of emperors were in their hands. For he declared that the god who had given him the purple (and he showed it in his right hand) had also fixed, beyond doubt, the length of his reign. And he did not desist until he had taken vengeance on fifty of the leaders of the revolt.

blocks: When Carus had risen in revolt, Probus took counsel what he ought to do. And as all were silent, a certain Martinianus, a tribune, speaking freely, reproached him at length, saying that affairs were being ruined by his sluggishness; and he urged him to move at once, go out to war and meet the usurper.

blocks: They say that Carus, at the moment of his proclamation, said that they had come to the throne to the Persians' cost.
text: They say that Carus, at the moment of his proclamation, said that they had come to the throne to the Persians' cost.

blocks: 1. At his own proclamation Diocletian, calling to witness the gods then worshipped, said that he wished to do away with Carinus not for the sake of the throne but out of pity for the state. 2. Doing many things brings about many reversals and dangers. 3. Human nature knows better how to bear adversity than how to keep measure in good fortune. 4. And for this reason one who has won undying honour must remember that he is mortal and no stranger to human misfortunes. 5. Lucius Octavius, invited to a triumphal dinner and then uninvited, sent word that he would come to the banquet if the finest possible portions were not sent to him. 6. Diocletian, when a vision in his sleep often troubled him, bidding him hand over an office to a certain man, whom the vision named, suspected that this came from sorcery, and one day sent for the man and said only this to him: "Take the office that you ask of me every night, and do not grudge the emperor the comfort of a quiet rest."

blocks: Licinius would not accept the gold coins on which Constantine had stamped his victory over the Sarmatians, but melted them down and turned them to other uses, answering those who blamed him for it only that he did not want barbarian work circulating in the dealings of his own realm. 2. Crispus, the son of Constantine, showed great feats of valour, and Licinius, defeated by him many times, in his vexation would say these verses of Homer (Il. 8.102): "Old man, the young fighters wear you hard indeed; your strength is loosed, and hard old age is upon you." 3. Tiberius proposed to the senate that Christ should be a thirteenth god; but the senate did not accept it, so that someone said in jest: "You do not accept him as the thirteenth, and he comes first."

blocks: Constantine planned first to move the seat of government to Serdica; and loving that city, he used to say again and again: "My Rome is Serdica." 2. Constantine, wishing to obscure the deeds of those who had reigned before him, was eager to belittle their virtues with certain nicknames. For he called Octavian Augustus fortune's ornament, Trajan the wall-plant, Hadrian a painter's tool, Marcus a laughing-stock, Severus***.
